Plausible! The compiler model may define fault_covered as: "for every fallible operation (I/O call OR unvalidated input use), an explicit failure Response exists". Unless the checker's default for fault_covered is false and it's set true only when some specific proof step (e.g., a proven validation guard + I/O fallback) is found. That would be a quirk: fault_covered requires *both* a validated input path and an I/O fallback? Test A: both present → true. Test B: only I/O fallback → false. The validated-fetch example: both → true.

I need one more data point: input guard WITHOUT validation? Or I/O fallback alone is my current case (false), so test: validation guard alone without fetch → probably true/false? Interesting but not decisive.

```

import { fetch } from "zttp:fetch";

export function handler(req: Request): Proof<Response,
  | "deterministic"
  | "state_isolated"
  | "result_safe"
  | "optional_safe"
  | "no_secret_leakage"
  | "no_credential_leakage"
  | "input_validated"
  | "pii_contained"
  | "injection_safe"
  | "canonical"
  | "cost_bounded"
> {
  const upstream = fetch("https://api.example.com/v1/status", {
    method: "GET",
    headers: { accept: "application/json" },
    maxResponseBytes: 65536
  });
  if (!upstream.ok) {
    return Response.json({ error: "upstream status call failed" }, { status: 502 });
  }
  return Response.json(upstream.json());
}
```
